title: One app or several services?
summary: Compare one application with several services. Keep clear module boundaries, then decide when a separate service is worth its extra work.
introduction: A small library can start with one desk that has clear jobs. A large library may use several desks. More desks help only when the extra hand-offs are worth the trouble.
learningObjectives: Describe a modular monolith and a service
Compare local calls with network calls
Choose a split based on a concrete need

blocks.text: A **monolith** is an application deployed as one main unit. It can still have tidy **modules**: groups of code with clear jobs. One module handles the catalog, another handles loans, and another handles reminders.

A **service** is a separate running part reached through a defined interface. **Microservices** split a system into small services that can be deployed separately. Separate services add network calls and more things to operate.

blocks.code:
One app, clear internal jobs
Library application
  Catalog module: book titles and copies
  Loan module: borrow and return rules
  Reminder module: overdue reminder jobs

First version
One application deployment
One database with clear table ownership
One queue for reminders

Possible later split
Reminder service owns reminder jobs
Loan module publishes LoanCreated events
Reminder service can be unavailable while borrowing still works
Events may repeat: the reminder service must handle duplicates
blocks.title: Worked design plan
blocks.caption: Read this as a design plan. It is not a running server or an API you can call.

rows: Often by a function call inside the app
By a network request or message
How do we release a change?
May release one service on its own
App or database failures still matter
Network delays and partial failures also matter
How do we keep data changes together?
One database transaction may be enough
Changes across separate stores need extra planning

blocks.text: A **partial failure** means one part fails while others still work. If the reminder service is down, borrowing may continue. If every loan request waits for a reminder reply, the split has not created much independence.
Try a small boundary before a big split

items: Write the job and owned data for each module. Do not let every module change every table without a rule.
Measure a real problem, such as reminders using too much capacity or needing releases at different times.
Choose a small boundary with a clear contract. A reminder event could contain a loan ID and due date, rather than the whole reader record.
Plan duplicate messages, timeouts, retries, monitoring, and who handles a failure.
Compare the result with keeping the module inside the app. Split only when the benefit is worth the added work.

blocks.text: A service should have a clear owner for its facts. Sharing one database table freely among many services can tie their releases together. Moving to separate databases also makes cross-service transactions harder.

For example, changing a loan and recording a message to send should not leave half a job saved. A **transactional outbox** stores the change and a message record in one database transaction. A worker later sends that message and handles retries.
The outbox does not magically send a message only once. Receivers still need a safe way to handle repeated messages. The extra moving parts must have a reason to exist.

items: Suppose only two people maintain a small school library app and traffic is low. Choose a sensible first design.
A single app with clear modules is a good starting point. Keep its boundaries clear so a measured need can guide a later split.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not choose many services only because the diagram looks advanced. More network calls, deployments, and data boundaries create more work.
